title: Be a renunciant at home
hookLine: re man aiso kar sanniaasaa: make your home your forest, your heart your hermitage (Dasam, Ramkali Patshahi 10)

cards: It's an old fantasy: quit the job, sell the stuff, move to a cabin in the mountains, and finally become the calm, deep person ordinary life never leaves time for.
In India, that dream has an old and honored form: the sannyasi, the renunciant who leaves home for the forest, with matted hair and ashes on the skin.
Guru Gobind Singh wrote a shabad that takes every piece of that picture, one by one, and moves it indoors.

teach.b: The shabad is in Raag Ramkali, among the Tenth Guru's hymns in the Dasam Granth. It opens: re man aiso kar sanniaasaa. In paraphrase: O mind, practice renunciation like this.
Think of your whole house as the forest, and stay detached inside your own heart.
Then it goes through the renunciant's kit, item by item, giving each a new meaning. Make self-control your matted hair. Make union with God your daily bath.
Let your teacher be wisdom, and smear the Name on yourself like ashes. Eat little, sleep little, love mercy and forgiveness.
Keep a gentle, contented nature, and keep lust, anger, pride, greed and attachment out of the mind. It's a clever move. The shabad doesn't mock the renunciant.
It takes the forest life seriously, then says the real forest is a way of living, and you can carry it into a kitchen.
That's a deep thread in Sikh teaching, running back to Guru Nanak, who lived as a householder and taught that God is found in the middle of ordinary life, not by escaping it.
The word for the inner detachment here is udaas: unattached, free inside.

teach.h: A CLEARING IN A FULL HOUSE.
teach.b: You can be udaas in a crowded house, and caught in a quiet cave.
So the question isn't where you live. It's whether, in the middle of the noise, there's a small clearing inside you where the Name is remembered.

how: Sikhs sing re man aiso kar sanniaasaa in kirtan as a picture of the householder's path: detachment and devotion lived inside family and work.

o: a hermit living in the forest
a mind full of worldly cares

games.q: the hermit's kit, indoors — tap the pairs.

s: the shabad mocks people who leave for the forest
it takes the forest life seriously and moves its meaning indoors.
Sikh teaching honors the householder's life
from Guru Nanak on, God is sought in ordinary life, not by escaping it.

games.q: you want to renounce the world and find God. where does the Tenth Guru's shabad tell your mind to go?
o: to a cave in the mountains.
nowhere: think of your house as the forest, and be unattached within.
games.why: the shabad keeps the renunciation but moves it home: self-control as matted hair, the Name as ashes.

practice: Stay exactly where you are, without tidying anything, and let the room be the forest: hear its sounds, the fridge, traffic, someone in the next room, as if they were birds and wind. Sit as still as a hermit would, feet rooted.
If you pray, say Waheguru in the clearing you've made.

wordCard.voice: Udaas, unattached, free inside: the Tenth Guru's shabad says think of your house as the forest, stay udaas within, and wear self-control, mercy and the Name as the hermit's marks.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: renunciation; re man aiso kar sanniaasaa, O mind, renounce like this.

carryVoice: Your line: the forest at home. A clearing inside, even in a full house. That's day six hundred seventy-three.

sources.ref: Ramkali Patshahi 10, Shabad Hazare (re man aiso kar sanniaasaa)
